## Source and status

Every parameter in this tool comes from one published, openly licensed study:

> Palacios A, Espinola N, Gonzalez JM, Rojas-Roque C, Rivas MM, Kanevski D, Morisset P,
> Augustovski F, Pichon-Riviere A, Bardach A. **Budget impact analysis of venetoclax for the
> management of acute myeloid leukemia from the perspective of the social security and the
> private sector in Argentina.** *PLoS One*. 2024;19(1):e0295798.
> [doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0295798](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0295798) — CC-BY 4.0.

This is a **methods demonstration**, not a client deliverable, not a validated reimbursement
model, and not a pricing recommendation. It contains no confidential or commercial data.
Market shares in the source are projections supplied by the manufacturer and validated by a
Delphi panel of six onco-haematologists; they are not observed market data.

Every input carries a source tag — a table number, a stated derivation, or an explicit
assumption. There are three assumptions and they are labelled as such.
:::

## What a budget impact model actually is

A cost-effectiveness model asks whether a therapy is worth its price. A budget impact model
asks a narrower and more immediate question: **can this payer afford to adopt it, and when
does the money move?**

The answer is a subtraction:

> the world **with** the new therapy, minus the world **without** it

That subtraction is the whole model. It is also where most of the difficulty sits, because the
two worlds must be built on the same population, the same time horizon and the same cost
categories, and only then differenced. Without an explicit market share layer there is only one
world and no budget impact at all — which is why that layer, not the headline number, is the
part worth inspecting first.

## The rebuild

The tool below reconstructs the published model from its parameters rather than restating its
results. Seven layers, in the order a reviewer would work through them:

1. the **epidemiology funnel**, from covered lives to treatable patients
2. **market share** in both worlds, year by year — the layer that makes it a budget impact model
3. **cost per patient per year**, in six components, built bottom-up
4. **budget impact**, annual and cumulative, with per-member-per-month
5. **one-way sensitivity analysis**, against the published tornado
6. **reconciliation** with the published results, including where it does not agree
7. **provenance** for every parameter

Three things surfaced during the rebuild that are worth naming, because they are the parts a
spreadsheet would hide:

- **The published supplement contradicts itself.** S1 Table and S7 Table assign the venetoclax +
  decitabine and venetoclax + LDAC market shares in opposite order. Reconciling each against the
  drug costs in Table 4 settles it, and the model follows the assignment that reproduces the
  published spend.
- **Drug cost had to be rebuilt as a function of treatment duration**, not taken as a fixed annual
  total. Duration is the leading sensitivity driver in the source; with a frozen annual cost it
  cannot move the result at all, and the sensitivity analysis would be theatre.
- **Calibrating to force agreement made the answer worse.** Correcting each cost component to
  match the published levels distorts the difference between the two worlds — which is the only
  quantity a budget impact model reports. The rebuild is left uncalibrated and the residual is
  shown.

## Technical notes

The tool is a static page: three JavaScript files, no server, no build step, no dependencies.
The separation is deliberate and is part of the point.

- `bim_params.js` — every parameter, each with a source tag. No logic.
- `bim_engine.js` — pure calculation. No DOM, no globals, parameters passed in, so the
  sensitivity analysis perturbs a copy rather than the base case.
- `bim_ui.js` — rendering and event binding only.

A reviewer who wants to audit the model does not need to read the interface code. They open the
parameter file and check it against the paper — which is the same thing they would ask to do
with a spreadsheet, and rarely can.

## Limitations

Three years, 28-day cycles, deterministic, no probabilistic sensitivity analysis — matching the
source. No QALYs or ICERs: this is a budget impact model, and mixing the two questions is a
common way to answer neither. Costs are US dollars at 2020 prices with no inflation adjustment,
following the source's stated reason for excluding it. Administration and hospitalisation do not
fully reconcile to the published figures because the unit costs they depend on are not reported;
the gap is quantified in the reconciliation panel rather than closed by fitting.
